newsitem.title: INDIA: India minister wants farm policy to boost reforms.
newsitem.headline: India minister wants farm policy to boost reforms.

text.p: India should reform its agriculture sector to strengthen its wider programme of economic change, senior officials said on Monday.

"Any economic reforms programme in India cannot be fully successful till timely and fundamental reforms are carried out in the agriculture sector," Food Minister Devendra Prasad Yadav told a meeting on reforms in the agriculture sector.
Agriculture employs about two-thirds of India's work force and accounts for about a third of its gross domestic product.
Industry officials said at the meeting, organised by the Confederation of Indian Industry (CII), that India needed to look at agriculture from a global perspective.
India has attained near self-sufficiency in foodgrains after a green revolution launched in the 1960s and 1970s.
A foodgrain importer until the early 1980s, India has been exporting foodgrains after an increase in output to 190.4 million tonnes in 1995/96 (April-March) from 50.8 million in 1950-51.
But agriculture ministry officials say only 46 million hectares has been brought under irrigation as part of the green revolution, out of a total 142 million hectares available to agriculture.

"It has become imperative to look at options that the green revolution either ignored or left unattended in its pre-occupation with technology," a CII-backed task force on future strategies in agriculture said on Monday.
The task force recommended that government should allot degraded land for reclamation and cultivation, either to the private sector or cooperatives.
It said small and marginal farms must be consolidated for either collective or cooperative farming.
The report said a large chunk of agricultural growth during the past few years could be attributed to good monsoons. India has enjoyed nine consecutive good monsoons.
It said agriculture's share of GDP had dropped to 31.1 percent in 1994/95 from 44.5 percent in 1970/71, mainly due to a steep fall in investment.
"A large chunk of the expenditure on agriculture was in the form of subsidies for fertilisers, irrigation, electricity, credit and other inputs rather than on capital formation," the CII report said.
A task force official said the government must find methods to rationalise its subsidies and farm input support policies to release more resources for capital formation in agriculture.
